newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: IMF's Camdessus says Latin banks shaky - report.
newsitem.headline: IMF's Camdessus says Latin banks shaky - report.

text.p: Latin America's crisis-prone banks are still not healthy enough to be sure of avoiding new shocks, International Monetary Fund (IMF) chief Michel Camdessus warned in a newspaper interview published Monday.

Asked by a group of papers including Argentina's El Cronista in Washington whether the shrapnel of banking crises were still troubling the region, Camdessus replied "Yes, sir. They accuse me of being alarmist. Maybe I haven't been convincing enough in what I've been shouting out."

"But if you look at these countries, each one has suffered, more or less severely, a banking crisis in the last few years. I think the worst is over, and that lessons have been learned and now what was decided about rules on financial prudence and banking supervision has to be implemented," he said.
Camdessus said no country in the region had completely healthy banks.
Latin America's financial systems were most recently shaken by the crisis unleashed by Mexico's December 1994 peso devaluation.
Among the hardest hit were Argentina's banks, some of which teetered on the financial brink for several months.

Camdessus repeated his support for the Argentine government's attempts to push through laws to dynamize its labor market, including measures to make work contracts more flexible. But he stressed the government should negotiate the changes with unions, which have successfully used legal action to block an attempt to pass the measures by decree.

"In a country like Argentina, where there is a grave problem with unemployment, it is very important that labor legislation does not get in the way of the creation of new jobs," he said. "So the reforms are something which it is worth putting to the unions and discussing with them."

He said he supported the economic policies of the government of President Carlos Menem and his moves to reduce corruption, and added, "If the government keeps up these efforts, we will not have any problems continuing to support them through our extended-fund facilities."
